deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivations. It is a page of aphoristic notes, apparently preparation for a lecture or essay on the nature of mathematical work. Its content, in order:

(1) It ends a thought experiment. The thought begins at the bottom of the transcription labelled 'next page' ("Wenn Jemand ohne alle Vorbildung, ohne Lesen und Schreiben zu können, nach Hören meiner Vorlesung, die ...") and continues at the top of this page ("... Lösung des Riemannschen Primzahlproblems brächte, so wäre er mir willkommner als Alle mit der besten Vorbildung"). In English: if someone with no preparation at all, unable even to read and write, brought the solution of Riemann's prime-number problem after hearing my lecture, he would be more welcome to me than all those with the best preparation. Presumably he would then recognise for himself the necessity of reading and writing and fill this gap in his education. The 'Riemann prime number problem' means the Riemann hypothesis: all nontrivial zeros of zeta(s) have Re(s) = 1/2. Hilbert treated it as the paradigm of a central open problem; it was Problem 8 of his 1900 list. The point is that results count, not formal credentials.

(2) After a dividing rule, a new aphorism. When choosing problems, regard for applications must never be decisive ("darf niemals die Rücksicht auf die Anwendung den Ausschlag geben").

A marginal and interlinear insertion adds a biblical image (Genesis 25, Esau selling his birthright for a dish of lentils). It reads roughly: "Wer würde wohl um das Linsengericht einer wohlgelungenen physikalischen Anwendung oder Anregung das Erstgeburtsrecht (der wissenschaftlichen Selbständigkeit) verkaufen". In English: who would sell the birthright (of scientific independence) for the mess of pottage of a successful physical application or stimulus? The insertion is followed by a small numeral '5.', apparently a section or ordering mark.

(3) A quotation, paraphrased from d'Alembert's preface to the Traité de dynamique (1743). The most abstract notions, which the ordinary person regards as the most inaccessible, are often precisely those that carry the greater clarity. This matches the original: "les notions les plus abstraites, celles que le commun des hommes regarde comme les plus inaccessibles, sont souvent celles qui portent avec elles une plus grande lumière."

Hilbert then adds his own rider: "Ich füge hinzu dass sie oft nicht die schwierigsten sind", i.e. such abstract notions are often not the most difficult. This fits his known methodological creed that the more general or abstract formulation of a problem is frequently the easier one. He states this in the 1900 Paris address, where generalisation often renders a problem more tractable.

There is nothing to compute. No implicit steps need filling.

deep.surprise_reason: These are philosophical and methodological lecture notes. They are fully consistent with Hilbert's known published views: the 1900 problems address, his anti-utilitarian stance on problem choice, and abstraction as simplifying. The witty Esau metaphor and the exact d'Alembert citation are pleasant archival details but not substantively new.
